app.title: 医析台 MedBench — local clinical data analysis workbench
app.summary: A person loads an Excel workbook of cases, picks a sheet and sets how its header and title rows are read, or opens a saved project. They check an overview of data quality, the structure it found and the analyses it recommends. They fix the table where needed: variable types, wide-to-long reshaping, missing-value imputation, outlier cleaning and joins across sheets, with undo. Then they run descriptive statistics, group comparisons, regression and survival models, and causal-inference methods across tabbed pages. They add only the results they want to the report, generate a methods paragraph from what was actually done, and export a Word report with journal-style tables, plus an Excel results file and a figure pack.

task.text: Take a table of clinical cases from raw spreadsheet to statistical results and a journal-ready analysis report.

data.text: A spreadsheet of cases with one row per patient or observation and one column per variable. Variables can be numeric, categorical, binary, date or text. A workbook can hold several sheets, one per dimension, linked by an identifier.
data.item: a patient or observation row in a case table

stage.text: analyzing a cleaned clinical case table and writing up the results for a paper

mechanism.text: A sidebar loads the data and sets how it is read, and shows the current dataset's summary. A row of tabs steps through overview, preparation, analysis families and report export. On each tab the person picks variables in forms, runs a method and sees its tables and figures, and an explicit 'add to report' button sends that result to a report cache that the export page orders, annotates and saves.

field.text: biostatistical analysis of clinical research and quality-control data in medicine

workflow.name: take a table from raw import to analyses and a written report

steps.here: Upload an Excel file, choose a sheet, and set the header rows, the title rows to skip and whether merged cells fill downward, with an 8-row preview. Alternatively, load the sample dataset or open a saved project file.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: The overview shows sample size, variable counts, missing rate and duplicates. It lists the structural roles it detected (groups, outcomes, time, pairing) and recommends analyses with their criteria, each with an 'open' button that jumps to the page.

steps.step: find and fix problems in the data
steps.here: The preparation page lets the person override variable types, reshape wide tables to long ones and impute missing values with single values or MICE. It also diagnoses table layout and applies chosen fix-up steps, and joins sheets by key with aggregation. Outliers can be kept, winsorized or dropped, and every change can be undone.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: On the descriptive, inference, time-and-QC, modeling and paper-support tabs, the person picks variables and runs tests (t, ANOVA, chi-square), agreement measures, regressions (linear, logistic, Cox, LASSO), PSM/IPTW, subgroup analyses or Table 1. Each method has its own diagnostics and figures.
Results only display until the person presses 'add to report'. That section, or a group of related figures, then goes into the report cache.

The export page assembles a methods paragraph from what was actually done (sample, missing handling, outliers, methods used). It keeps an analysis ledger, and can optionally ask an AI to review the analyses or draft results and methods text.

The person ticks the chapters, chooses Chinese or English and a journal table/figure template, and generates a Word report with three-line tables. Results can also go out as an Excel workbook or a 300 dpi PNG/TIFF image pack, and the whole session can be saved as a project file.

distinctive: Results go into the report only when the person asks. Browsing tabs never adds chapters, and a model's result is kept only while its parameters are unchanged.
The methods paragraph is built only from operations actually performed, so the write-up cannot describe methods that do not appear in the results.
Joining one-to-many sheets requires an aggregation rule and is rolled back if the row count changes, which guards against inflating the sample size.

Optional AI help receives only a structural summary (field names, types, unique counts, missing rates) and never data rows. Its suggested methods are set against a local rule engine and marked where they agree or disagree.
Tables and figures follow journal conventions: three-line tables, p-value formatting, numbered captions, set figure widths and 300 dpi output.
